items.title: UK adds 13 designations and 6 specifications under the Russia sanctions regime
items.summary: On 6 August 2026 the UK Sanctions List was updated with 13 new designations and 6 new specifications under the Russia regime, the latest in a steady run of additions through July and August.
items.whyItMatters: Banks with a UK nexus should refresh sanctions screening lists to capture the new Russia-regime designations and specifications promptly, to avoid processing transactions for newly listed persons or entities.

sources.name: UK Sanctions List

items.title: HMRC names and fines Petrofac Facilities Management for Russia sanctions breaches
items.summary: HMRC publicly named Petrofac Facilities Management Limited (PFML) on 29 June 2026 after it accepted a £569,157 compound settlement for supplying sanctioned industrial goods and technical assistance to Russia-connected individuals during 2022-2023, while winding down its Russian operations. It is the first time HMRC has publicly named a firm accepting this type of settlement.
items.whyItMatters: The public naming signals a new HMRC enforcement posture for strategic-export and sanctions violations; banks financing or servicing exporters winding down Russia-exposed operations should reassess due-diligence expectations around self-reporting and technical-assistance exposure.

sources.name: HMRC: Energy firm named after £500,000 Russia sanctions settlement

items.title: OFSI's Lukoil wind-down licences approach expiry in August 2026
items.summary: OFSI's general licences permitting continued business with Lukoil International entities (INT/2025/8031092, extended to 25 August 2026) and Lukoil Bulgaria entities (INT/2025/7895596, extended to 13 August 2026) are both due to lapse this month; the international-entities licence was also amended to remove the frozen-account payment restriction in paragraph 4.2. (Confidence: medium — corroborated via legal-sector reporting on the licence text rather than a direct read of the licence document itself.)
items.whyItMatters: Banks with counterparties relying on these licences to continue Lukoil-linked business need to confirm wind-down completion or a further extension before the licences lapse, or transactions risk falling outside authorised activity.

sources.name: OFSI General Licences

items.title: OTSI publishes guidance on banknote sanctions with Russia and Belarus
items.summary: On 3 August 2026 OTSI published guidance on complying with sanctions relating to banknotes, covering the prohibition on providing banknotes to persons connected with Russia or Belarus (including postal and hand-carried transfers), with a £10,000 personal-travel exception.
items.whyItMatters: Retail and private banking teams handling customer cash withdrawals or currency exchange tied to travel to Russia or Belarus should align controls with the new £10,000 personal-use threshold and the guidance's due-diligence expectations.

sources.name: OTSI: Complying with sanctions relating to banknotes

items.title: OFAC designates Iran-linked individuals and issues amended Iran FAQ
items.summary: On 7 August 2026 OFAC added Iran-related and counter-terrorism designations to the SDN list, including Saeed Ghasempour and Amir Hendi, removed certain counter-narcotics designations, and issued an amended Iran-related FAQ (FAQ 1257). (Confidence: medium — the full designee list and the FAQ's substance were not independently confirmed beyond the two individuals identified.)
items.whyItMatters: US-nexus banks should refresh OFAC screening lists for the new Iran-related SDN entries and review amended FAQ 1257 for any change to permitted-activity guidance.
entities: Saeed Ghasempour (also known as Sa'id Ghasempur)

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions

items.title: OFAC sanctions crypto exchanges and a front-company network tied to Iran's IRGC
items.summary: On 7 August 2026 OFAC sanctioned seven entities and five individuals, including two UAE-based exchange houses, for helping Iran's banking system move hundreds of millions of dollars and supporting the IRGC, including alleged support for Shahr Bank's efforts to repatriate oil-sale revenue.
items.whyItMatters: Digital-asset and correspondent-banking teams should screen counterparties against the newly designated exchange houses and front companies, and reassess exposure to UAE-based crypto exchanges used in Iran-linked flows.

sources.name: US Treasury: Treasury Sanctions Crypto Exchanges Funding Iran's IRGC and Enabling Illicit Finance

items.title: OFAC removes 84 SDN entries and updates 22 more in second modernization round
items.summary: On 27 July 2026 OFAC completed the second round of its sanctions-list modernization initiative (announced by the Treasury Secretary in May 2026), removing 84 individuals and entities, primarily deceased persons, defunct entities and decades-old listings, improving identifying data on 22 entries, and consolidating 18 duplicate entries.
items.whyItMatters: Screening teams should reconcile watchlists against the delisted and consolidated entries so false-positive alerts on outdated SDN records are cleared, and confirm no active relationships were incorrectly blocked against superseded entries.

sources.name: US Treasury: Treasury Announces Second Round of Sanctions Removals, Updates in Modernization Initiative

items.title: OFAC settles Iran sanctions case with Rice Lake Weighing Systems for $60,764
items.summary: On 12 August 2026 OFAC announced a $60,764 settlement with Wisconsin-based Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. over eight apparent violations: its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to a UAE distributor between July 2019 and November 2021 knowing the goods would be re-exported to an end-user in Iran.
items.whyItMatters: A reminder that OFAC enforcement reaches indirect re-export exposure through foreign subsidiaries; trade-finance teams should verify end-use and re-export controls for goods routed through UAE intermediaries toward Iran.

sources.name: OFAC: Settlement Agreement with Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc.

items.title: EU adopts 21st sanctions package against Russia, its largest listing round yet
items.summary: On 23 July 2026 the Council of the EU adopted its 21st sanctions package against Russia: 218 additional listings (48 individuals, 170 entities), the highest number since the war began. From 13 August 2026, transaction bans extend to 33 more Russian financial institutions plus banks in Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia and India; from 25 August 2026, Russian nationals are barred from sitting on the boards of any EU crypto-asset services business. The package also expands energy, trade and military-industrial restrictions.
items.whyItMatters: The 13 and 25 August transaction-ban and crypto-board effective dates give banks a narrow window to unwind or restructure relationships with the newly listed financial institutions and crypto-asset businesses before the prohibitions take effect.

sources.name: European Commission: EU adopts 21st package of sanctions against Russia
Council of the EU: 21st package of sanctions

items.title: UN 1267 Committee amends the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
items.summary: On 13 August 2026 the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) enacted amendments to entries on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List (asset freeze, travel ban and arms embargo). (Confidence: low — which specific entries were amended could not be confirmed: main.un.org and press.un.org both blocked automated access during this run, so this item rests on secondary search corroboration rather than the primary notice.)
items.whyItMatters: Any amendment to the 1267 list can affect identifying details on existing screening matches; banks should pull the current ISIL/Al-Qaida list rather than rely on cached data until the specific change is confirmed.

sources.name: UN Security Council: Sanctions List Materials (1267 Committee)

items.title: UK adds 6 new designations under the Global Human Rights and Counter-Terrorism regimes
items.summary: On 8 September 2026 the UK Sanctions List was updated with 5 new designations under the Global Human Rights regime and 1 new designation under the Counter-Terrorism (International) regime, according to the list's published change log. The Global Human Rights regime entries were further varied on 9 September and corrected on 10 September; the change log does not name the individuals or entities involved.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should refresh Global Human Rights and Counter-Terrorism (International) regime screening lists to capture the new designations and the follow-up variation/correction made in the days after.

sources.name: UK Sanctions List

items.title: UK amends 21 entries on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaeda sanctions list
items.summary: On 20 August 2026 the UK Sanctions List recorded 21 variations to entries under the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaeda regime, the largest of several amendments to this regime in the period — 4 further variations were made on 17 August, 1 on 7 September, and 1 correction on 10 September. The published change log gives counts only, not which entries or individuals were affected. (Confidence: medium — the specific entries changed were not independently confirmed beyond the change-log counts.)
items.whyItMatters: Any amendment to this regime's entries can affect identifying details on existing screening matches; banks should pull the current ISIL/Al-Qaeda list rather than rely on cached data.

sources.name: UK Sanctions List

items.title: UK makes further Russia regime amendments, including one revocation, plus minor Afghanistan regime changes
items.summary: Between 27 August and 21 September 2026 the UK Sanctions List recorded a further run of amendments: 2 variations under the Afghanistan regime (27 August), 1 more (28 August), 4 amendments under the Russia regime (2 September), 1 amendment (3 September), 1 variation (10 September), 1 variation (11 September), and 1 revocation — a de-listing — under the Russia regime (21 September). The published change log gives counts only, not which entries or individuals were affected.
items.whyItMatters: The 21 September revocation is a de-listing that should be reflected in screening records promptly; the other entries are amendments to existing listings that may affect identifying details on current screening matches.

sources.name: UK Sanctions List

items.title: OTSI publishes its Annual Review for 2025-26
items.summary: On 28 August 2026 the Office of Trade Sanctions Implementation (OTSI) published its Annual Review for the 2025-26 financial year, covering compliance engagement, licensing and enforcement activity, with the Russia sanctions regime as a key focus. The review highlights the implementation of new Sanctions End-Use Controls in May 2026 and the expansion of OTSI's licensing remit in April 2026 to cover exports of sanctioned goods and ancillary services, in addition to its existing remit over sanctioned services.
items.whyItMatters: OTSI's expanded remit — now covering licensing for sanctioned goods exports, not just services — and the new End-Use Controls change what trade-sanctions compliance teams need to screen and license for; worth reviewing current processes against the updated scope.

sources.name: OTSI Blog: Annual Review 2025-2026

items.title: UK lays major Iran sanctions amendment regulations, in force 29 September 2026
items.summary: The Iran (Sanctions) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/983), made on 7 September 2026, substantially expand the UK's Iran sanctions regime and come into force on 29 September 2026. New provisions include financial-sector prohibitions on lending, correspondent banking, insurance and dealing in Iranian government-guaranteed bonds issued after 8 September 2026; new trade prohibitions on gold, precious metals, diamonds, energy-related goods and technology, and sectoral software; new banknote-export and oil-tanker-related prohibitions; and new ship and aircraft measures including UK port-entry and landing restrictions for Iran-connected vessels and aircraft.
items.whyItMatters: This is a broad expansion of the Iran sanctions framework spanning financial services, trade and shipping/aviation; banks should review Iran-connected lending, correspondent banking, insurance, bond, trade-finance and vessel-related exposure against the new prohibitions before they take effect on 29 September 2026.

sources.name: The Iran (Sanctions) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/983)

items.title: US removes Syria's State Sponsor of Terrorism designation and delists HTS
items.summary: On 24 August 2026 the US State Department removed Syria's designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism, lifting prohibitions under the Terrorism List Governments Sanctions Regulations. The State Department also revoked Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham's (HTS, formerly al-Nusrah Front) designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organisation, and OFAC removed HTS from the SDN List and revoked the related Syria General License 25 as no longer necessary. Commerce, State and Treasury issued an updated Tri-Seal Advisory on Syria sanctions and export-control relief.
items.whyItMatters: This substantially changes the Syria sanctions landscape; banks with restricted or heightened-scrutiny policies tied to Syria's former SST status or to HTS/Syrian-government links should reassess those policies and screening rules, including reliance on the now-revoked Syria GL 25.

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions: Removal of Syria's designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism

items.title: OFAC designates a large Iran-linked network of individuals, shipping and front companies
items.summary: On 24 August 2026, alongside the Syria/HTS action, OFAC added numerous individuals and entities to the SDN List under Iran-related sanctions authorities (including E.O. 13846, E.O. 13902 and the Iran-related non-proliferation authority), spanning Iran-based cyber actors, senior Iranian figures including Amir Hatami and Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, and a Turkey/UAE/Hong Kong/Singapore/China network of shipping and trading companies including Good Luck Shipping LLC and Amdeh Ship Management and Operation Co. L.L.C. OFAC also published a new E.O. 13902 sectoral determination covering aviation, digital-asset, gold, shipping and technology sectors of the Iranian economy, suspended Iran General Licenses F and G, and issued new Iran General Licenses AA and BB.
items.whyItMatters: The scale and geographic spread of this round (UAE, Hong Kong, Singapore, China, Turkey) means correspondent-banking and trade-finance teams with counterparties in those jurisdictions should screen against the new SDN entries, particularly shipping and trading front companies, and review use of the now-suspended Iran GLs F and G.
entities: Amdeh Ship Management and Operation Co. L.L.C.

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions: Iran-related Designations

items.title: OFAC delists Ethiopia sanctions program participants as underlying national emergency expires
items.summary: The national emergency declared in Executive Order 14046 (September 2021), concerning the humanitarian and human rights crisis in Ethiopia, has expired. On 18 September 2026 OFAC removed from the SDN List the individuals and entities designated under that programme — including the People's Front for Democracy and Justice, the Eritrean Defense Forces, Red Sea Trading Corporation and Hidri Trust — and removed the programme's FAQs from its website.
items.whyItMatters: Ethiopia/Eritrea (E.O. 14046) sanctions screening flags should be retired for the delisted parties; banks maintaining blocked-property records tied to this programme should confirm the delisting before continuing to treat these parties as blocked.
entities: People's Front for Democracy and Justice

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions: Expiration of Emergency With Respect to the Situation in Ethiopia

items.title: OFAC issues general licence authorising negotiations for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH
items.summary: On 18 September 2026 OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131J, authorising certain transactions for the negotiation of and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities, alongside two amended Russia-related FAQs (1224 and 1225).
items.whyItMatters: This is a US-side counterpart to the Lukoil wind-down activity already being tracked on the UK side (OFSI's Lukoil general licences); banks with Lukoil International-linked exposure should review GL 131J's scope before relying on it for sale-related transactions.

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions: Issuance of Amended Russia-related General License

items.title: OFAC tightens Iran licensing policy and settles $1.43m Iran sanctions case under Operation Economic Outcast
items.summary: On 10 September 2026 OFAC modified its Iran-related specific-licensing policy to a presumption of denial, with narrow exceptions (e.g. risk to life, limb or environmental safety), as part of Operation Economic Outcast. Separately, OFAC announced a $1,427,230 settlement with an individual who provided management-consulting and advisory services to a leading Iranian software company, received Iranian-origin dividends into US bank accounts, and acquired Iranian real property; OFAC found the apparent violations egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed.
items.whyItMatters: Teams handling Iran-related specific-licence applications should expect a presumption of denial going forward; the settlement is a reminder that indirect Iran exposure through consulting services, dividend receipts and real-property acquisition falls within OFAC's enforcement scope.

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions: Licensing Policy Update and Settlement Agreement

items.title: OFAC designates Kata'ib Hizballah and Hizballah-linked financial networks in Iraq, Lebanon and the UAE
items.summary: On 10 September 2026 OFAC added individuals and entities to the SDN List linked to Kata'ib Hizballah in Iraq and a Hizballah financial network in Lebanon, including exchange houses and general-trading companies — Shams and Bahr Trading Company L.L.C. (Dubai), Gold Pro SARL (Beirut), Yousef Ibrahim Mansour and Partner for Exchange (Lebanon), and Ain Al Iraq for Protection Systems Technology and Audio, Visual, and Communications Solutions Company Ltd (Baghdad) — under the Hizballah Financial Sanctions Regulations and related counter-terrorism authorities.
items.whyItMatters: Correspondent-banking and trade-finance teams with Iraq, Lebanon or UAE exposure should screen against the new entries, particularly exchange houses and general-trading companies used as Hizballah-linked financial conduits.

items.title: OFAC designates VTB Bank, one of Russia's largest banks, for Iran sanctions evasion
items.summary: On 14 September 2026, under Operation Economic Outcast, OFAC designated VTB Bank Public Joint Stock Company — one of Russia's largest financial institutions — pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. Treasury said VTB Bank opened offices in Iran, established correspondent banking relationships with sanctioned Iranian banks, moved billions in frozen Iranian assets, and built a rial/ruble settlement system to expand bilateral trade. VTB was previously designated under Russia-related authorities (E.O. 13662 in January 2025 and E.O. 14024 in February 2022).
items.whyItMatters: Foreign financial institutions that continue dealing with VTB Bank now face secondary sanctions risk under Iran authorities on top of existing Russia-related exposure; banks should confirm no correspondent or other relationships with VTB remain in place and review counterparties for indirect exposure.
entities: VTB Bank Public Joint Stock Company

sources.name: US Treasury: Operation Economic Outcast Sanctions Major Bank Helping Iran Evade Sanctions

items.title: OFAC designates BitBank and the Zanjani digital-asset network funding the IRGC
items.summary: On 17 September 2026 OFAC designated BitBank, an Iranian digital-asset exchange controlled by OFAC-designated financier Babak Zanjani, along with its developer Pishtaz Simorgh Electronic Trade Company and three Zanjani associates — Hossein Ali Zaker Hossein, Mohammad Mahdi Zaker Hossein and Seyed Adel Heidari — under E.O. 13902's digital-asset-sector authority. OFAC said BitBank was used since June 2026 to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars in Bitcoin to the IRGC on behalf of OFAC-designated Hormuz Safe Marine Services Authority.
items.whyItMatters: Digital-asset and correspondent-banking teams should screen counterparties against BitBank and the newly designated Zanjani-network entities and individuals, and treat Iranian digital-asset exchanges generally as elevated sanctions-evasion risk per OFAC's guidance (FAQ 1250, FAQ 1257).
items.programme: Iran / digital assets — Operation Economic Outcast

sources.name: US Treasury: Operation Economic Outcast Disrupts Digital Asset Exchange Enabling the Iranian Regime

items.title: EU extends Ukraine territorial-integrity sanctions listings for three years, delists a handful of individuals
items.summary: On 22 September 2026 the Council of the EU prolonged the restrictive measures targeting those responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence for a further 36 months, until 22 September 2029. The listings apply to more than 3,000 individuals and entities. As part of the review, the Council decided not to renew the listings of three individuals and one entity, and removed three deceased persons from the list.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should update screening records for the delisted and non-renewed entries while continuing to treat the roughly 3,000 extended listings as in force through 2029.

sources.name: Council of the EU: Ukraine's territorial integrity: EU extends individual listings for three years

items.title: EU lists five more individuals over Russia's military-industrial complex
items.summary: On 7 August 2026 the Council of the EU adopted restrictive measures against five individuals holding senior positions at Russian defence and military-technology companies, including Ramil Nailevich Badgutdinov (General Director of JSC Serpukhov Plant Metallist, which produces components used in Russia's Iskander-M missile system) and Aleksandr Yurevich Dyukarev (General Director of JSC Krasnoyarsk Machine-Building Plant, which produces the RS-28 Sarmat missile system), plus directors of companies producing military communications systems and UAV/space-related military technology.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should screen for the newly listed individuals and review any exposure to the Russian defence-industrial companies they lead.

sources.name: Council of the EU: Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine: EU lists five additional individuals supporting Russia's military-industrial complex

items.title: EU sanctions Prince Holding Group, Jin Bei Group and DKBA over Southeast Asian scam centres
items.summary: On 30 July 2026 the Council of the EU imposed restrictive measures under its Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime on seven persons and three entities responsible for serious human rights violations tied to scam-centre operations in Cambodia and Myanmar, including human trafficking and torture of trafficked workers. Those listed include the Prince Holding Group and its chairman Chen Zhi, the Jin Bei Group and its chairman Zhu Zhongbiao, and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), a Burmese armed group that controls territory where scam-centre compounds operate.
items.whyItMatters: The Prince Holding Group's cryptocurrency investment-scam operations reach victims globally; correspondent-banking, payments and crypto-facing teams should screen for the newly listed entities and individuals.
items.programme: EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime

sources.name: Council of the EU: Scam centres in Southeast Asia: EU lists seven persons and three entities responsible for serious human rights violations

items.title: EU sanctions six more individuals over Iran human-rights violations
items.summary: On 24 July 2026 the Council of the EU sanctioned six additional individuals over serious human-rights violations in Iran: five judges of Iran's Revolutionary Courts who presided over trials of religious minorities and political dissidents — including Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi — imposing death sentences, long prison terms and flogging; and Nima Salehi, an Iranian hacker and founder of the 'Ashiyane' cyber group linked to the IRGC and Iran's Cyber Police. The EU's Iran human-rights sanctions now cover 269 individuals and 53 entities.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should screen for the newly listed individuals under the EU's Iran human-rights sanctions regime.

sources.name: Council of the EU: Iran: Council sanctions an additional six individuals over serious human rights violations

items.title: UN 1267 Committee amends 21 entries on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
items.summary: On 18 August 2026 the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) amended 21 entries on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List, updating identifying details on previously listed individuals. The changes include confirming Isnilon Totoni Hapilon (QDi.204) as killed in the Philippines in October 2017, and correcting aliases and other identifying details for entries including Nurjaman Riduan Isamuddin, also known as Hambali (QDi.087).
items.whyItMatters: Banks should refresh cached copies of the ISIL/Al-Qaida list to capture the updated identifying details, including death confirmations that may resolve stale screening matches.

sources.name: UN Security Council Press Release SC/16435

items.title: UN sanctions committees make further technical amendments to Taliban and ISIL/Al-Qaida list entries
items.summary: On 27 August 2026 the 1988 Committee (Taliban sanctions) amended one entry, updating identifying details for Abdul Salam Hanafi. On 4 September 2026 the 1267 Committee amended two ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida entries, updating identifying details for Sanaullah Ghafari (a.k.a. Shahab al Muhajir, leader of ISIL-Khorasan) and Abubakar Swalleh (an ISIL facilitator in East and Southern Africa). Both changes are identifying-detail corrections rather than new designations.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should refresh cached copies of the Taliban and ISIL/Al-Qaida lists to capture the updated identifying details on these existing entries.

sources.name: UN Security Council Press Release SC/16443
UN Security Council Press Release SC/16446

items.title: Security Council renews Sudan sanctions for one month, to 9 October 2026
items.summary: On 11 September 2026 the Security Council adopted resolution 2828 (2026), renewing the Sudan sanctions measures (arms embargo, travel ban and asset freeze under resolutions 1556, 1591 and 2035) only until 9 October 2026, and extending the 1591 Committee's Panel of Experts until 9 November 2026. It was followed by resolution 2830 (2026) on 8 October. (Updated 4 November 2026: the earlier version of this item could not confirm the resolution's content; it has now been read from the primary text.)
items.whyItMatters: A one-month rollover rather than the usual annual renewal signals Council disagreement over the regime's future; banks screening against the UN Sudan list should track each renewal.

UN Security Council: Resolutions adopted 2026

items.title: UK adds 31 Russia regime listings, including LNG carriers and Georgian politicians
items.summary: On 1 October 2026 the FCDO added 31 entries to the UK Sanctions List under the Russia regime: individuals including Georgian politicians from the Solidarity for Peace party (such as Mamuka Pipia, who led a delegation to meet the head of the so-called Donetsk People's Republic), eight ships carrying Russian-origin liquefied natural gas to third countries (including the ALEKSEY KOSYGIN, KONSTANTIN POSIET and PYOTR STOLYPIN), and Novatek Gas and Power Asia Pte Ltd, designated for operating in Russia's energy sector. The UK Sanctions List change log records the round as 23 designations and 8 specifications.
items.whyItMatters: Trade-finance, shipping and correspondent-banking teams should screen for the newly specified LNG carriers and Novatek's Singapore trading arm, which signal UK pressure on Russian LNG exports through third-country intermediaries.
entities: Novatek Gas and Power Asia Pte Ltd

items.title: UK designates Zarubezhneft, Kyrgyz payment firms and shadow-fleet tankers in 38-entry Russia round
items.summary: On 8 October 2026 the FCDO added 38 entries under the Russia regime, including Zarubezhneft JSC (designated as a Government of Russia-affiliated energy company), Russian bank Commercial Bank "Stolichny Kredit", Kyrgyzstan-registered financial-services firms OJSC Processing KG, Tokenspot CJSC and Tsunami Payments LLC, suppliers based in China, Turkey and Canada, and twelve tankers carrying Russian-origin oil to third countries. The same notice varied the existing listings of Rostec and HeliCo Group. OFSI issued a wind-down general licence for Zarubezhneft and its subsidiaries (INT/2026/11080040), which expires at 23:59 on 21 November 2026.
items.whyItMatters: Banks with exposure to Zarubezhneft or its subsidiaries have until 21 November 2026 to wind down under the OFSI licence; the Kyrgyz payment and token firms point to continuing use of Central Asian payment rails to move Russia-linked funds, which correspondent-banking teams should screen for.

items.title: UK designates two individuals over Iranian state hostile activity
items.summary: On 12 October 2026 the FCDO added two individuals under the Iran (Sanctions) Regulations 2023: Ruhollah Bazghandi, for planning or conducting espionage and attacks against persons and assets on behalf of the Government of Iran, and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, for supporting attacks against persons in countries other than Iran.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should add both individuals to screening under the UK's Iran hostile-activity regime.

sources.name: FCDO Sanctions Notice, Iran, 12 October 2026

items.title: UK designates 15 SAF and RSF commanders over atrocities in Sudan
items.summary: On 26 October 2026 the FCDO designated 15 individuals under the Sudan regime, with asset freezes, travel bans and director disqualification. They include Sudanese Armed Forces officers and allied commanders linked to violence against civilians in Gezira State and Wad Madani (such as Major General Awad Al-Karim Ali Saeed and Abu Zaid Talha Al-Misbah of the Al-Baraa bin Malik Battalions), and Rapid Support Forces commanders linked to the takeover of El Fasher and Zamzam camp, including sexual violence (such as Abbas Khater Bakhit and Khademallah Khashmin Herika).
items.whyItMatters: The round targets both sides of the conflict; banks with Sudan, Gulf or East Africa exposure should screen for all 15 names and their aliases.

sources.name: FCDO Sanctions Notice, Sudan, 26 October 2026

items.title: UK replaces its Global Human Rights regime with a wider human rights and IHL sanctions regime
items.summary: The Global Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law Sanctions Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/1071) came into force on 15 October 2026. They establish a regime covering serious human rights violations by or on behalf of a State, serious violations of international humanitarian law, and obstruction of humanitarian assistance. The Regulations revoke the Global Human Rights Sanctions Regulations 2020 and include transitional provision for existing designations. A separate Order (S.I. 2026/1089) extends the regime to British overseas territories other than Bermuda and Gibraltar.
items.whyItMatters: Screening systems and internal policies that reference the 2020 Global Human Rights regime by name need updating to the new regime, and the broader designation criteria (IHL violations, obstruction of aid) widen the pool of potential future designations.
items.programme: Global Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law

items.title: OFSI extends the Lukoil Bulgaria general licence to February 2027
items.summary: On 28 October 2026 OFSI extended General Licence INT/2025/7895596, which permits continued business with Lukoil's Bulgarian entities, to 26 February 2027. According to the publication notice, the licence now covers Lukoil Bulgaria EOOD, Lukoil Neftochim Burgas AD, Lukoil Aviation Bulgaria EOOD and Lukoil Bunker Bulgaria EOOD.
items.whyItMatters: Banks relying on this licence for Lukoil Bulgaria-related business have a new 26 February 2027 end date and should check that activity involving the aviation and bunkering subsidiaries falls within its terms.

sources.name: OFSI Publication Notice: INT/2025/7895596 (October 2026)
OFSI General Licences

items.title: OFSI issues a new Legal Services General Licence replacing INT/2026/9512597
items.summary: On 26 October 2026 OFSI added Legal Services General Licence INT/2026/11112108, taking effect after the previous licence (INT/2026/9512597) expired on 28 October 2026. It lets UK law firms and counsel receive payment from designated persons for legal advice without a specific licence across most UK autonomous regimes. The main changes clarify the definition of Expenses, including payments to other legal professionals, and change the expenses cap wording from 10% of fees "payable" to 10% of fees "paid".
items.whyItMatters: Banks processing legal-fee payments from frozen accounts under the general licence should update references to the new licence number and check the revised expenses terms.

items.title: UK delists entries under ISIL/Al-Qaida, Iraq and Syria regimes, alongside routine amendments
items.summary: Between 29 September and 3 November 2026 the UK Sanctions List change log recorded several removals and amendments: 1 revocation under the Syria regime (6 October), 1 delisting under the Iraq regime (7 October), 3 delistings and 3 variations under the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida regime (27 October), 5 amendments under the Afghanistan regime (30 October), and a series of variations and corrections under the ISIL/Al-Qaida, Russia and Libya regimes. The change log gives counts only, not which entries were affected.

items.title: Treasury imposes over $1.21bn in penalties on Bank of America, including an $11.6m OFAC settlement
items.summary: On 13 October 2026 Treasury announced enforcement actions totalling more than $1.21 billion against Bank of America: a FinCEN penalty for failing to report and mitigate national-security risks, an OCC civil money penalty of $750 million for a deficient BSA/AML programme, and an OFAC settlement of $11,662,930 for apparent violations of sanctions programmes covering Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism. OFAC said the bank routed correspondent payments through blocked banks, let designated individuals make payments and withdrawals because of poorly calibrated sanctions alerts, failed to update watchlists promptly after designations, and mishandled accounts linked to blocked persons. OFAC found the violations non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, and gave no reduction for remediation or cooperation.
items.whyItMatters: The OFAC findings map directly onto common bank control gaps: alert calibration, watchlist update latency and correspondent payment routing. Compliance teams should test their own controls against each failure OFAC described.
items.programme: Multiple (Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, terrorism)

items.title: OFAC warns foreign banks they can be sanctioned without notice for dealing with Iran
items.summary: On 5 October 2026 OFAC published an alert, "Notice to Foreign Financial Institutions Conducting Business with Iran", stating that foreign financial institutions that continue to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could be targeted at any time without advance notification and should terminate such activity immediately. The alert presents Operation Economic Outcast's earlier bank actions as precedent (FinCEN's proposed rule against Banque Misr UAE, OFAC's designations of Golden Global Bank and VTB Bank; each has its own item) and points institutions to existing Treasury guidance on Iranian shadow-banking typologies.
items.whyItMatters: This is an explicit secondary-sanctions warning to non-US banks; correspondent-banking teams should review respondent banks' exposure to Iranian banks and their third-country branches, and apply the shadow-banking typologies the alert references.

items.title: Treasury designates the Russia-linked A7 shadow banking network and proposes cutting off its sub-agents
items.summary: On 1 October 2026 Treasury took coordinated action against the A7 Network, a shadow banking network with ties to Russia that Iran has used to evade sanctions. OFAC designated the network as a significant transnational criminal organisation; FinCEN proposed a rule that would prohibit transmittals of funds involving the network's sub-agents, and issued an alert to help financial institutions detect related activity. Treasury said the sub-agents are third-country companies built to disguise sanctioned payments as ordinary commerce using falsified trade documents. The action builds on OFAC's August 2025 designation of A7 LLC and Old Vector LLC. The proposed rule's comment period closes 30 days after Federal Register publication.
items.whyItMatters: If finalised, the FinCEN rule would bar US institutions from processing funds transfers involving A7 sub-agents; banks should apply the FinCEN alert's red flags now and consider commenting on the proposal.

items.title: OFAC designates Iraqi, offshore Iranian and Cuban banks serving Iran
items.summary: On 15 October 2026 OFAC designated Iraq-based International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, which Treasury said provided US dollar access to Iran and ties to Iran-aligned militias, along with Iranian offshore banks including Chabahar International Bank Overseas Company and Jazireh International Bank Company, plus exchange houses and individuals in Iran's shadow banking network. The State Department concurrently designated Cuba-based Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA), which Treasury said has served designated Iran-based Karafarin Bank since at least 2022. OFAC issued Iran General License FF to wind down transactions with the Iraqi bank, amended as FF-1 on 29 October.
items.whyItMatters: Correspondent-banking teams should check for nested or direct exposure to the Iraqi, offshore Iranian and Cuban banks named, and use GL FF-1 only within its wind-down terms.

items.title: FinCEN alerts banks to Iranian abuse of religious charity networks and khums payments
items.summary: On 15 October 2026 FinCEN issued an alert asking financial institutions to report potential Iranian regime abuse of religious charity networks, including diversion of religious tithes (khums), which Treasury said the regime uses to enrich elites, fund repression and support terrorism abroad.
items.whyItMatters: Banks serving religious charities or diaspora communities with links to Iran or neighbouring countries should add the alert's indicators to transaction monitoring and SAR guidance.

items.title: OFAC extends Iran sectoral sanctions to the automotive and rail sectors
items.summary: On 1 October 2026 OFAC published a determination under Executive Order 13902 covering the automotive and rail sectors of the Iranian economy, exposing persons operating in those sectors to sanctions, and designated Iranian industrial firms and foreign suppliers including Heavy Equipment Production Company (HEPCO) and HEPCO Shanghai Co. Treasury said the automotive sector is intertwined with IRGC patronage networks, trade-based money laundering and the use of prison labour.
items.whyItMatters: Trade-finance teams should treat Iranian automotive and rail sector counterparties and their foreign suppliers as sanctionable under E.O. 13902 going forward.

items.title: OFAC targets Iran's remaining shadow fleet, including a Panama- and Greece-based law firm
items.summary: In two rounds on 8 and 21 October 2026, OFAC designated ship managers, shipping companies and tankers in what Treasury described as the vast majority of Iran's remaining shadow fleet. The 21 October round included Panama- and Greece-based law firm Karnakis and Karnakis, which Treasury said supported illicit Iranian shipping for years, together with Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading S.A. and Whales Shipping Line LLC. OFAC issued wind-down general licences for India-based Samudra Marine Services (GL EE) and for certain persons and vessels blocked on 21 October (GL HH).
items.whyItMatters: Designating a law firm extends shadow-fleet risk to professional service providers; trade-finance and maritime-lending teams should rescreen ship managers, vessels and service providers in their Iran-adjacent maritime exposure.

items.title: OFAC removes 125 SDN entries in third modernization round
items.summary: On 5 October 2026 OFAC completed the third round of its sanctions-list modernization initiative, removing 125 individuals and entities, including deceased individuals, defunct companies and entries lacking enough information for reliable screening, and updating 22 list entries to improve screening.
items.whyItMatters: Screening teams should reconcile watchlists against the removals and updated entries to clear stale alerts and confirm no current relationships were blocked on superseded data.

items.title: OFAC consolidates enforcement and penalty rules into new Sanctions Penalties Regulations
items.summary: On 24 September 2026 OFAC published a new part of 31 CFR chapter V, the Sanctions Penalties Regulations, consolidating enforcement procedures and penalty information, including the rights of US persons under investigation, that previously sat in individual programme regulations; more than 100 subparts will be replaced by cross-references. OFAC also amended the Terrorism List Governments Sanctions Regulations to reflect the rescission of Syria's State Sponsor of Terrorism designation, removing a Syria-specific general licence.
items.whyItMatters: Compliance manuals and policies that cite penalty provisions in individual programme regulations should be updated to reference the consolidated Sanctions Penalties Regulations.

items.title: OFAC renews Lukoil general licences for retail stations, Bulgaria and the Lukoil International sale
items.summary: On 15 October 2026 OFAC issued Russia-related General License 128D (transactions involving Lukoil retail service stations outside Russia) and 130B (transactions involving certain Lukoil entities in Bulgaria). On 21 October it issued General License 131K, the next version of the licence authorising negotiation of and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH, with amended FAQs 1224 and 1225.
items.whyItMatters: Banks relying on earlier versions of these licences (including 131J, issued 18 September) should update to the current versions and check their terms before processing Lukoil-related transactions.

items.title: OFAC sanctions Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society over M23 support
items.summary: On 28 October 2026 OFAC sanctioned Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution that Treasury said played a key role in facilitating Rwanda's support for the M23 armed group in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and its political wing, the Congo River Alliance. Treasury framed the action as holding Rwanda to its commitments under the Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity.
items.whyItMatters: Designating a state ministry and a domestic financial institution raises exposure for banks with East African correspondent or trade-finance relationships; teams should check for direct and nested exposure to Zigama.

items.title: OFAC makes designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act
items.summary: On 19 October 2026 OFAC added Beijing-based venture capital vehicles associated with Qiji Chuangtan (MiraclePlus), including Qiji Chuangtan Beijing Investment Management Co Ltd and its Phase I and Phase II funds, together with Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Co Ltd, to its Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022. The listed measures include blocking of property (except for imports of goods) and a cap on loans from US financial institutions. OFAC issued PAIPA General Licenses 1 and 2, the latter authorising wind-down of transactions with the listed entities. OFAC's action notice does not state the grounds for the listings.
items.whyItMatters: The PAIPA measures appear on the Non-SDN Menu-Based list, not the SDN List; banks need that list in screening to catch these entities, and should check the US-lender loan cap for any credit exposure.

items.title: OFAC designates Tren de Aragua fraud network that stole millions from US banks
items.summary: On 30 September 2026 OFAC designated 10 targets involved in a Tren de Aragua fraud scheme that Treasury said stole millions from US banks and has become a key revenue source for the group, a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization. The scheme is led by Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre ("Prometheus"), one of the FBI's ten most-wanted fugitives; OFAC also designated senior leader Juan Gabriel Rivas Nunez ("Juancho").
items.whyItMatters: Fraud-prevention and sanctions teams should connect: losses from this scheme fall on US banks, and the designations make any funds traced to the network blocked property.

items.title: OFAC settles with Extreme Networks ($1.53m) and Pegasus Worldwide Logistics ($175k)
items.summary: On 27 October 2026 OFAC announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., which exported networking equipment and services on nine occasions between 2018 and 2022 to a Russian defence manufacturer blocked by operation of law as majority-owned by designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey; OFAC found the violations egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed. On 9 October OFAC settled with freight forwarder Pegasus Worldwide Logistics for $175,015 over dealing in blocked property under the Illicit Drug Trafficking Sanctions Regulations and failing for six months to respond fully to an OFAC subpoena.
items.whyItMatters: Extreme Networks shows how 50%-ownership blocking catches unlisted subsidiaries; Pegasus shows that a slow or incomplete response to an OFAC subpoena is itself a penalised violation.

items.title: EU adopts its largest-ever listings package against Russia: 1,569 companies and CEOs
items.summary: On 12 October 2026 the Council of the EU listed 1,569 individuals and entities in Russia's military-industrial complex, 826 companies and 743 individuals serving as their chief executives, under the regime protecting Ukraine's territorial integrity. The Commission said it is the single largest set of EU listings ever, bringing the regime close to 4,600 listings. The targets are mid-level suppliers of components for missiles, UAVs and aircraft, including semiconductors, radars, satellite systems, explosives and navigation systems, with combined annual turnover of at least €20 billion.
items.whyItMatters: The volume and the focus on lesser-known component suppliers mean screening lists need a full refresh, and trade-finance teams should expect more true matches among Russian industrial counterparties.

items.title: FinCEN proposes cutting Banque Misr UAE off from US correspondent banking
items.summary: On 28 August 2026, under Operation Economic Outcast, FinCEN proposed a rule that would revoke Banque Misr UAE's correspondent banking access to US financial institutions. Treasury estimated the bank processed about $1.8 billion between January 2024 and June 2026 for 103 companies potentially part of Iranian shadow banking networks, including apparent front companies for Iran's Ministry of Defense and the IRGC. The same day OFAC designated Reza Mohammad Taeedi, general manager of Bank Melli's Dubai branch, and Hong Kong-based Kameng Trading Limited, which Treasury said laundered funds for sanctioned exchange house Pedram Pirouzan (Opal Exchange). The action against Banque Misr UAE is a proposed rule, not an SDN designation.
items.whyItMatters: If finalised, US institutions could no longer maintain correspondent accounts for Banque Misr UAE; banks with direct or nested exposure to it should assess that exposure now, and screen for the two OFAC designations.

items.title: OFAC designates Türkiye-based Golden Global Bank for serving the IRGC-Qods Force
items.summary: On 4 September 2026, under Operation Economic Outcast, OFAC designated Türkiye-based Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi Anonim Sirketi (Golden Global Bank) and its subsidiaries, including Golden Global Portfoy Yonetimi A.S., under E.O. 13902 for operating in Iran's financial sector. Treasury said the bank facilitated tens of millions of dollars in transactions for the IRGC-Qods Force and gave the Iranian regime correspondent banking access to move funds internationally. OFAC issued Iran General License CC authorising the wind-down of transactions with persons blocked that day.
items.whyItMatters: Correspondent-banking teams with Turkish exposure should screen for the bank and its subsidiaries and confirm any remaining activity falls within GL CC's wind-down terms.

items.title: Executive Order implements the Graham Russia–Iran sanctions act, then waives its tariffs and most sanctions
items.summary: On 16 October 2026 the President issued an Executive Order implementing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which the order says was signed into law on 18 September 2026. The order sets duty increases provided for by the Act (500% on goods from Russia; 100% on goods from the largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas and from the top facilitators of Russian oil sanctions evasion), then waives all of the Act's duties and most of its sanctions provisions, citing a national-interest certification to Congress. The waivers stay in effect until the President or Secretary of State determines further action is appropriate. The order states it does not affect existing Russia sanctions under prior Executive Orders. It delegates the Act's authorities to State, Treasury, Energy and the US Trade Representative.
items.whyItMatters: Nothing changes for banks today, but the statutory authority for broad Russia- and Iran-linked secondary measures now exists and can be switched on by lifting the waivers; teams should watch for USTR monitoring reports and any withdrawal of the waivers.

items.title: Security Council rolls Sudan sanctions over again, to 11 December 2026
items.summary: On 8 October 2026 the Security Council adopted resolution 2830 (2026), renewing the Sudan sanctions measures (arms embargo, travel ban and asset freeze under resolutions 1556, 1591 and 2035) until 11 December 2026, and extending the 1591 Committee's Panel of Experts until 11 January 2027. It follows resolution 2828 (2026), which had renewed the measures only until 9 October 2026.
items.whyItMatters: Two short rollovers in a row put the Sudan regime on a short renewal cycle; banks screening against the UN Sudan list should watch for the December decision.

items.title: Security Council renews Haiti sanctions for a year and extends its Panel of Experts
items.summary: On 14 October 2026 the Security Council adopted resolution 2831 (2026), renewing for one year the Haiti sanctions measures in resolution 2653 (2022) (asset freeze, travel ban and targeted arms embargo) and extending the Panel of Experts for 13 months, with an interim report due by 28 March 2027 and a final report by 1 September 2027. The resolution also flags misappropriation, embezzlement and diversion of public resources as a risk to Haiti's stability.
items.whyItMatters: The Haiti regime and its listings stay in force into October 2027; banks with Caribbean exposure should keep the 2653 list in screening.

items.title: OFAC publishes new Cuba sanctions regulations and amends the Cuban Assets Control Regulations
items.summary: On 29 September 2026 OFAC published regulations implementing Executive Order 14404 of 1 May 2026 ("Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and Threats to the United States National Security and Foreign Policy") and amended the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (31 CFR part 515), effective on Federal Register publication on 30 September 2026. It issued five new and 29 amended Cuba-related FAQs and an OFAC alert, "Expanded Sanctions Against Cuba", on increased sanctions risk for Cuba-related transactions. In the same release OFAC amended the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations to incorporate E.O. 13902 and removed over 100 duplicative subparts from its CFR chapter.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should review Cuba-related payment and trade-finance policies against the amended CACR and the new E.O. 14404 regulations; the State Department's later designation of Cuba-based BICSA under E.O. 14404 shows the authority is already in use.

items.title: OFAC authorises transactions in Russian-origin diesel fuel until April 2027
items.summary: On 9 October 2026 OFAC issued Russia-related General License 135, authorising transactions prohibited under the Russian Harmful Foreign Activities and Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations that relate to the sale, delivery, offloading or importation, including into the United States, of diesel fuel of Russian Federation origin, through 12:01 a.m. EDT on 7 April 2027. The licence does not authorise any debit to an account at a US financial institution of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation, the National Wealth Fund or the Ministry of Finance.
items.whyItMatters: Trade-finance teams may see Russian-origin diesel transactions that are now licensed; payments still cannot be debited from the excluded Russian state accounts, so checks on the paying account remain necessary.
